definition: Sharp and stinging in tone, especially when criticizing or joking.
example: The coach's acerbic remarks about sloppy passing stung, but the team practiced harder all week.
nuance: Acerbic suggests a sharp, sour wit that stings; caustic implies harsher words meant to wound or corrode.
prompt: A theater critic writes a review of a play she found painfully dull.
options: Her acerbic column called the second act a long nap with costumes.
Her acerbic column praised every actor with warm, gentle compliments.
The acerbic smoke from the fog machine made the front rows cough.
Her acerbic column simply listed the play's running time and ticket prices.
reasons: A cutting joke that mocks the play's dullness has exactly the sharp, stinging edge the word requires.
Warm, gentle praise has no sting, so it is the opposite of the intended tone.
This confuses the word with acrid, which describes harsh smells; acerbic describes words or temperament.
A neutral list of facts carries no bite or criticism at all.

practice.prompt: A retired chef serves as the judge at a neighborhood baking contest.
options: The acerbic judge hugged each baker and declared every pie a masterpiece.
Before judging began, the bakers stretched through an acerbic workout to stay limber.
The acerbic judge offered only a timid, mumbled "nice job" to every entry.
With acerbic wit, the judge said one pie crust could double as a roof shingle.
reasons: Affectionate, glowing praise is the reverse of a sharp, stinging manner.
This mixes up the word with aerobic, which describes exercise, not a harsh tone.
A shy, bland comment has no edge, so it misses the word's cutting quality.
A pointed, mocking joke about a tough crust shows sharp, stinging humor.
